sentences.text: The name Hypacrosaurus translates to "near the highest lizard," reflecting its massive size which was just slightly smaller than that of Tyrannosaurus.
This dinosaur possessed a tall, hollow, rounded crest that was less large and straight than the crest of Corythosaurus, yet it featured a small bony point at the rear.
Neural spines projected from the top of its vertebrae, reaching heights five to seven times greater than the vertebral bodies to create a tall back in profile.
As a duck-billed dinosaur, it shared a striking resemblance with the genus Corythosaurus.
The genus remained obscure until 1987, when nests, eggs, and hatchlings of H. stebingeri were discovered in the Bear Paw Formation.
A large, single-species group of Hypacrosaurus stebingeri in Montana was interpreted as a herd killed by a volcanic ash fall.
Hypacrosaurus stebingeri laid spherical and rough eggs measuring 20 by 18.5 centimeters containing embryos 60 centimeters long.
The genus Hypacrosaurus was described and named by Brown in 1913.
The type remains, which served as the holotype for the species, were collected in 1910 by Barnum Brown for the American Museum of Natural History.
Hypacrosaurus was a herbivore that alternated between bipedal and quadrupedal positions.
Its skull allowed for a grinding motion analogous to chewing, utilizing teeth packed in dental batteries containing hundreds of teeth, though only a few were in use at any time.
The animal cropped plants with a broad beak and held them with a cheek-like organ, feeding from the ground up to about 4 meters above.
Hypacrosaurus stebingeri laid roughly spherical eggs containing embryos that were 60 cm long, and hatchlings were approximately 1.7 meters long.
Research by Lisa Cooper and colleagues suggests Hypacrosaurus stebingeri could have reached reproductive maturity at 2 to 3 years old and maximum size between 10 to 12 years old.
The postulated growth rate for Hypacrosaurus stebingeri was faster than that of tyrannosaur predators like Albertosaurus and Tyrannosaurus.
The hollow crest of Hypacrosaurus likely served social functions, such as visual signaling for sex or species identification and providing a resonance chamber for sounds.
Oxygen-isotope ratios suggest Hypacrosaurus was a homeotherm and likely endothermic, though this contradicts earlier findings based on nasal turbinates.
Hypacrosaurus is classified as a lambeosaurine hadrosaurid, a recognition made from the description of its skull.
It belongs to the subfamily Corythosaurini.
Hypacrosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately between 75 and 67 million years ago.
Remains of Hypacrosaurus species date from 75.0 to 69.5 million years ago and were found in Alberta, Canada, and Montana, United States.

The crest and nasal passages of Hypacrosaurus are subjects of debate regarding dinosaur endothermy and the presence of nasal turbinates, with some researchers arguing it was not warm-blooded based on the absence of these structures.

It is debated whether Hypacrosaurus is paraphyletic; Suzuki et al. suggested a strong relationship between Nipponosaurus and H. stebingeri in 2004, but Evans and Reisz rejected this in 2007, finding the two species form a separate clade from Nipponosaurus but with Corythosaurus and Olorotitan.
